title: Earth's four spheres
description: Scientists describe Earth as four overlapping spheres: rock (geosphere), air (atmosphere), water in every form (hydrosphere) and life (biosphere).

facts.text: Scientists describe Earth in spheres: the solid, rocky Earth (the lithosphere or geosphere), the atmosphere of air above it, the hydrosphere of water, and the biosphere, the parts of Earth where life exists, which overlaps all the others.
The hydrosphere is all of a planet's water, on the surface, underground and in the air, whether it is liquid, vapor or ice.

title: The spheres are linked
description: Earth's spheres trade water, gas and energy: plants move soil water into the air, and big eruptions put sulfur into the sky that cools the planet.

facts.text: In transpiration, roots take up water from the soil and leaves release it into the air as water vapor through tiny pores (stomata); a large oak tree can transpire about 40,000 gallons (151,000 liters) a year.

After big explosive eruptions, ash falls out of the stratosphere within days to weeks, but sulfur dioxide turns into sulfuric acid droplets that reflect sunlight; several eruptions in the past century cooled Earth's surface for one to three years.

title: What makes a mineral
description: A mineral is a natural solid with a set chemical recipe and an orderly arrangement of atoms, usually formed without living things. Ice qualifies; liquid water does not.

facts.text: A mineral is a naturally occurring, homogeneous solid with a definite chemical composition and a highly ordered atomic arrangement, usually formed by inorganic processes.
Ice, the solid form of water, qualifies as a mineral; liquid water does not.
Quartz is silica, silicon dioxide (SiO2), and its varieties include purple amethyst, yellow citrine, pink rose quartz and smoky quartz.

title: Rocks are made of minerals
description: A rock is a mix of one or more minerals. Scientists recognize just over 6,000 minerals, and common rocks like granite and sandstone are built from a few of them.

facts.text: A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals; common rocks include granite, basalt, limestone and sandstone, and common minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica and calcite.
The International Mineralogical Association recognizes just over 6,000 mineral species, and in recent years it has accepted more than a hundred new species a year.

title: The Mohs hardness scale
description: Mohs ranked ten minerals from talc (1) to diamond (10): a harder mineral scratches a softer one. The scale gives an order, not equal steps.

facts.text: The Mohs scale, devised in 1812 by German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs, ranks ten minerals by scratch hardness: talc (1), gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz (7), topaz, corundum and diamond (10); a harder mineral scratches a softer one.
On the Mohs scale a fingernail rates about 2.2, a copper penny about 3.2, a pocketknife about 5.1 and a glass plate about 5.5.
The Mohs scale is not linear: going from calcite (3) to fluorite (4) is roughly a 25% increase in hardness, while going from corundum (9) to diamond (10) is more than 300%.

title: Streak and luster
description: A mineral's streak (the color of its powder) is more reliable than its color, and its luster (how it reflects light) narrows the choices further.

facts.text: A mineral's streak is the color of its powder, made by scraping it across unglazed porcelain (a streak plate); the streak is usually more consistent than the mineral's apparent color, which can vary a lot.
Hematite ranges from red and brown to black, gray and silver, yet it always leaves a reddish streak; its name comes from the Greek word for blood.
Pyrite, nicknamed fool's gold for its gold color and metallic luster, leaves a greenish-black streak, while real gold leaves a yellow streak.
Luster describes how a mineral reflects light; a metallic luster looks like metal and belongs to opaque minerals such as pyrite and galena, while quartz usually has a vitreous (glassy) luster.

title: The crust's most common minerals
description: Silicate minerals, built on oxygen and silicon, make up most of the crust. Feldspars alone are more than half of it, and quartz comes second.

facts.text: Silicon and oxygen are the two most abundant elements in Earth's crust, and silicate minerals make up about 95% of Earth's crust and upper mantle.
Feldspars make up more than half of Earth's crust.
Quartz is the second most abundant mineral in Earth's crust after feldspar; it rates 7 on the Mohs scale and is highly resistant to weathering, so it concentrates in sandstones.

title: What granite is made of
description: Granite is mostly feldspar and quartz, often with flakes of mica, a mineral that splits into thin, elastic sheets.

facts.text: Granite's main minerals are feldspars and quartz, often with mica (muscovite or biotite); in some granites the feldspar is reddish orange and the quartz nearly white.
Mica's defining property is perfect cleavage into thin elastic sheets; biotite mica is black, brown or dark greenish brown.

title: Why sand is mostly quartz
description: Quartz is common, hard, has almost no cleavage and barely dissolves or decomposes, so it outlasts other minerals and ends up as most of the world's sand.

facts.text: Quartz is by far the commonest mineral in sand because it is abundant in rocks, comparatively hard, has practically no cleavage, is nearly insoluble in water and does not decompose.

title: Cooling rate and crystal size
description: Magma that cools slowly underground grows big crystals (intrusive rock); lava chilled fast at the surface makes tiny crystals (extrusive rock), or glass like obsidian.

facts.text: Intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks cool slowly deep in the crust, growing crystals big enough to see without magnification; extrusive (volcanic) rocks cool rapidly at the surface, giving microscopic crystals or glass.
Slow cooling deep underground gives ions time to migrate and build large crystals, while magma erupted at the surface is chilled so quickly that its minerals have little or no chance to grow.
Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass formed when viscous lava cools so rapidly that it solidifies before crystals can grow.

title: Granite versus basalt
description: Granite is coarse, light and intrusive, the typical rock of continents; basalt is fine-grained, dark, iron- and magnesium-rich and extrusive, the main rock of the ocean floor.

facts.text: Granite is a coarse- to medium-grained intrusive igneous rock that cools slowly at depth and is the most common plutonic rock of Earth's crust; continental crust is mostly granites.
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock, usually very fine-grained, dark and comparatively rich in iron and magnesium; oceanic crust is mostly basalts.
As a lava flow cools it contracts and cracks into columns, most of them six-sided; Devils Postpile in California is a famous example.

title: From sediment to rock
description: Loose sediment becomes sedimentary rock when layers are compacted and minerals cement the grains together. Such rocks cover most land but are a thin skin on the crust.

facts.text: Sedimentary rocks make up about 75% of Earth's exposed land surface but only about 5% of Earth's crust by volume.
Loose sediment becomes sedimentary rock through compaction under pressure and cementation, as minerals precipitate in the pore spaces between grains.

title: Sandstone, shale and limestone
description: Sandstone started as sand, shale as mud, and limestone largely as the shells of sea creatures. Shale is by far the most common.

facts.text: Sandstone is made of sand-sized grains, 0.063 to 2 mm across, mostly quartz, held together by a cement such as silica or calcium carbonate.
Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock of silt- and clay-sized particles that splits into thin layers; it is the most abundant sedimentary rock, roughly 70% of the total.
Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate, usually as calcite, and in many limestones the grains are microscopic fragments of fossil shells from lime-secreting sea life.

title: Metamorphic rock: changed, not melted
description: Heat, pressure and hot fluids transform existing rock without melting it. Limestone recrystallizes into marble, whose round calcite grains never line up in layers.

facts.text: Metamorphic rocks form when igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rocks are changed by high heat, high pressure or hot mineral-rich fluids; the rock does not melt but becomes denser and more compact as its minerals rearrange or react.
Marble is limestone or dolomite that has recrystallized under heat, pressure and fluids; its main mineral is calcite.
The marble for Michelangelo's David came from the Carrara quarries in Tuscany; he began carving on September 13, 1501, and finished in 1504.

title: Foliation: shale into slate
description: Pressure lines up flat minerals into parallel sheets (foliation). That turns shale into slate, which splits into thin slabs; schist and gneiss are foliated too.

facts.text: Foliation forms when pressure squeezes flat or elongate minerals in a rock so they line up; minerals that are not flat, such as those in limestone, cannot align, and rocks like gneiss and schist are strongly banded or foliated.
Slate is a fine-grained metamorphic rock formed from mudstone or shale; pressure gives it cleavage, so it splits into thin slabs used for roofing, flooring and blackboards.

title: What makes a gem
description: Gems are prized for beauty, durability and rarity. Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum, colored by different trace elements.

facts.text: Gemstones are minerals highly prized for beauty (from color, clarity, luster and optical effects), durability and rarity; durability means a stone keeps its polish and withstands constant handling, and some non-mineral materials such as pearl, coral and amber are also gemstones.

Corundum is aluminum oxide, rated 9 on the Mohs scale and second in hardness only to diamond; pure corundum is colorless, ruby is red corundum colored by chromium, and sapphire's blue comes from iron and titanium.

title: What makes an ore
description: An ore is rock with minerals that can be mined and sold at a profit: an economic label, not a geological one. Hematite is a key iron ore.

facts.text: An ore is a natural aggregation of minerals that can be mined and sold for profit; hematite and magnetite are ore minerals of iron, and chalcopyrite of copper.

'Ore deposit' is an economic term and 'mineral deposit' a geological one: every ore deposit is a mineral deposit but not the reverse, and whether a deposit pays depends on its concentration, size, mining and transport costs and market prices.

title: What soil is made of
description: Healthy soil is about half solids (mostly mineral bits sorted into sand, silt and clay, plus organic matter) and half pore space holding water and air. Five factors shape it.

facts.text: A typical soil in good condition is about 45% mineral matter, 25% air, 25% water and 5% organic matter; the mineral matter is tiny rock fragments classed by size as sand, silt and clay, and clay particles need a powerful microscope to see.
Soils are complex mixtures of minerals, water, air, organic matter and countless organisms, with organic matter being the decaying remains of once-living things.

A soil develops as its parent material weathers, shaped by five factors: parent material, climate, living organisms, topography and time; where all five are the same the soil is the same, and where any differs the soils differ.

title: Soil horizons
description: Dig a soil pit and you see layers: O (organic), A (topsoil), E (leached), B (subsoil), C (parent material) and R (bedrock, which is not soil).

facts.text: A soil profile is made of horizons: O (mostly organic matter such as decomposing leaves), A (topsoil, minerals mixed with organic matter), E (leached, missing in some soils), B (subsoil, where leached minerals accumulate) and C (parent material).
Under the C horizon lies R, bedrock such as granite, basalt, quartzite, limestone or sandstone; bedrock is not soil.

title: Quartzite: sandstone remade
description: Heat and pressure recrystallize quartz sandstone into quartzite, so tough that it breaks through its grains and resists weathering.

facts.text: Quartzite is sandstone converted into solid quartz rock, including by recrystallization under heat and pressure; it breaks through, not around, its sand grains, leaving a smooth surface, and it is extremely resistant to weathering, so it often stands up as hills.
